# Nehemiah 2 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview of the Chapter

Nehemiah 2 marks the transition from prayer to action. After four months of waiting, fasting, and praying (since Chisleu of Nehemiah 1:1), Nehemiah's opportunity comes. The chapter covers: his appeal to Artaxerxes (vv. 1–8), his journey to Jerusalem with royal backing (vv. 9–10), his secret nighttime survey of the ruined walls (vv. 11–16), his rallying of the Jewish leadership (vv. 17–18), and the first open opposition from Sanballat, Tobiah, and Geshem (vv. 19–20).

---

## v. 1 — The Date, the Setting, and Nehemiah's Sadness

*Now in the month of Nisan, in the twentieth year of King Artaxerxes, when wine was set before him, I took the wine and gave it to the king. I had never been sad in his presence…*

- **Nisan** (the old Abib) is the first month of the Jewish year, corresponding to March/April. Since Nehemiah 1:1 places the earlier events in Chisleu (November/December), roughly **four months of prayer and waiting** elapsed. (Ellicott, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/2.htm; Constable, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/nehemiah-2.html)

- **The cupbearer** was far more than a servant: he was a trusted bodyguard who tasted the king's wine to prove it was not poisoned, a man of proven character, and often a trusted advisor. Nehemiah held a position of tremendous influence and daily access. (Guzik/EnduringWord, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-2/)

- The **date** is significant for biblical chronology. Several commentators note that this decree (March/April 444 B.C.) marks the **starting point of Daniel's prophecy of the seventy weeks** (Daniel 9:25). Sir Robert Anderson calculated that exactly 173,880 days from this decree brings one to Christ's triumphal entry. (Guzik, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-2/; Constable, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/nehemiah-2.html)

- Nehemiah had **never been sad in the king's presence before** this. Persian court protocol required cheerfulness before the monarch; to appear sad could be interpreted as dissatisfaction with the king. (Pulpit Commentary, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/nehemiah-2.html; Guzik)

- The Pulpit Commentary suggests several possibilities for the four-month delay: perhaps the court had moved to Babylon for the winter, or Nehemiah had not been on duty, or he had been concealing his grief, waiting for God's providence to open the door. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/nehemiah-2.html)

---

## v. 2 — The King Notices; Nehemiah's Fear

*…so the king said to me, “Why is your face sad, though you are not ill? This could only be sadness of the heart.” I was overwhelmed with fear…*

- The king's question is notable for its **kindness**. Artaxerxes Longimanus, though a weak monarch politically, was personally kind-hearted. Most Persian monarchs would not have noticed a servant's sadness; a Xerxes might have ordered execution. (Pulpit Commentary, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/nehemiah-2.html)

- Nehemiah's fear sprang from the fact that **a sad countenance was not tolerated in the royal presence**. Though Artaxerxes was milder than other Persian kings, the abruptness of his question showed Nehemiah that the protocol was still in force. (Ellicott, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/2.htm)

- Constable adds that Artaxerxes could have interpreted sadness as **dissatisfaction with the king** (cf. Esther 4:2), and that Persian art shows those entering the king's presence did so with great deference, placing the right hand with palm facing the mouth so as not to defile the king with their breath. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/nehemiah-2.html)

- Guzik notes that Nehemiah was afraid not only for his life but because **so much was riding on this moment** — the answer to four months of prayer was at hand. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-2/)

---

## v. 3 — Nehemiah's Tactful Reply

*…and replied to the king, “May the king live forever! Why should I not be sad when the city where my fathers are buried lies in ruins, and its gates have been destroyed by fire?”*

- "May the king live forever" was a **common Oriental compliment** (cf. 1 Kings 1:31; Daniel 2:4). As cupbearer, Nehemiah had probably said it countless times, but now it carried special weight to conciliate the king. (Pulpit Commentary, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/nehemiah-2.html; Ellicott, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/2.htm)

- Nehemiah showed great **tact and wisdom**: he did not immediately name "Jerusalem," which had a bad reputation with Persian kings as a rebellious city. Instead he referred to "the city where my fathers are buried." (Guzik, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-2/)

- Ellicott notes that Nehemiah appeals to the **desecration of his fathers' sepulchres** — an appeal that had great force with Persians, who deeply respected tombs. Nehemiah does not yet betray the deepest desire of his heart (to rebuild), but simply states the cause of his grief. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/2.htm)

- Guzik adds that Nehemiah's answer was not only wise but **honest**. He didn't reply "Nothing's wrong" as we often do when asked about our troubles. He described the problem without blaming others. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-2/)

- The Pulpit Commentary notes that Nehemiah's warmth of feeling may **exaggerate** the fact that Jerusalem "lies waste" (since the temple had been rebuilt), but he may have been unconscious of the exaggeration. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/nehemiah-2.html)

---

## v. 4 — The King's Question and Nehemiah's "Arrow Prayer"

*“What is your request?” replied the king. So I prayed to the God of heaven…*

- Artaxerxes understood that Nehemiah's speech contained a complaint and that he must have a request. **With gracious kindliness he facilitates its utterance.** (Pulpit Commentary, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/nehemiah-2.html)

- **"So I prayed to the God of heaven"** — this is what Ellicott calls "the first note of that habit of ejaculatory prayer which is a characteristic of this book." It was a silent, instantaneous cry. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/2.htm)

- Guzik stresses that this prayer was **not long or extended** — it was an immediate, silent "Help me, LORD" prayer. Effective prayer does not always require length. This quick prayer rested on four months of extended praying and showed that Nehemiah depended on the Lord in every situation. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-2/)

- Constable calls this "a beautiful example of spontaneous prayer, one of the best in the Bible," and quotes Breneman: "Quick prayers are possible and valid if one has prayed sufficiently beforehand." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/nehemiah-2.html)

- The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary notes: "He did not fall down on his knees and begin begging God…The prayer was in his heart, from which place God could hear him as readily as though shouted in a loud voice. This teaches a lesson which Jesus and the apostles emphasized in the New Testament (Matthew 6:7; 1 Thessalonians 5:17)." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/nehemiah-2.html)

---

## v. 5 — Nehemiah's Bold Request

*…and answered the king, “If it pleases the king, and if your servant has found favor in your sight, I ask that you send me to Judah, to the city where my fathers are buried, so that I may rebuild it.”*

- Nehemiah framed his request with **humble courtesy**: "If it pleases the king…if your servant has found favor." He respectfully asked for a leave of absence and to be *sent* by the king — inviting the king to become a partner in the work. (Guzik, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-2/; Pulpit Commentary, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/nehemiah-2.html)

- Still, Nehemiah avoids naming "Jerusalem" directly; he says "Judah, to the city of my fathers' tombs." Guzik notes this is **not deceptive** — Jerusalem was no longer the rebellious city it once was. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-2/)

- Nehemiah's goal is explicit: **"that I may rebuild it."** He wasn't going on a fact-finding trip or to criticize the Jerusalem leaders. He went to get the work done. (Guzik)

- Constable notes that Nehemiah realized the moment had arrived for him to ask Artaxerxes to **revise his official policy toward Jerusalem** (cf. Nehemiah 1:11; Ezra 4:21) — a request that could itself have incurred the king's displeasure. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/nehemiah-2.html)

---

## v. 6 — The King's Favorable Response; The Queen Present

*Then the king, with the queen seated beside him, asked me, “How long will your journey take, and when will you return?” So it pleased the king to send me, and I set a time.*

- The **queen** (Hebrew *shegal*) is mentioned — probably **Damaspia**, the one legitimate wife of Artaxerxes Longimanus (according to Ctesias). Her presence indicates this was not a public feast (where the queen would be absent, as in Esther 1:9–12), but a more private occasion. (Ellicott, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/2.htm; Pulpit Commentary, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/nehemiah-2.html)

- The king's practical questions — "How long? When will you return?" — show he was **favorably disposed** and seriously considering the request. (Guzik, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-2/)

- **"I set him a time"** — Nehemiah had a definite plan. He didn't vaguely say "it's up to the Lord." The four months of prayer had been spent not only talking to God but **listening and working out a Spirit-led plan**. Guzik: "Faith is no substitute for planning." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-2/)

- Though Nehemiah set a time, circumstances later prolonged his stay to **twelve years** (Nehemiah 5:14), presumably with extensions of leave granted. (Pulpit Commentary; Ellicott)

---

## v. 7 — Letters for Safe Passage

*I also said to him, “If it pleases the king, may letters be given to me for the governors west of the Euphrates, so that they will grant me safe passage until I reach Judah.*

- Nehemiah was not content with permission alone. Once the king showed willingness, he **boldly asked for more**: official letters guaranteeing safe passage through the provinces "beyond the River" (west of the Euphrates). (Guzik, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-2/)

- Ellicott notes that between Susa and the Euphrates protection was not needed; it was **beyond the river** that travel became unsafe (cf. Ezra 8:31). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/2.htm)

- Constable observes: "Divine working and human planning are not necessarily contradictory." Nehemiah planned carefully and used proper channels. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/nehemiah-2.html)

---

## v. 8 — Timber Request; "The Good Hand of My God"

*And may I have a letter to Asaph, keeper of the king's forest, so that he will give me timber to make beams for the gates of the citadel to the temple, for the city wall, and for the house I will occupy.” And because the gracious hand of my God was upon me, the king granted my requests.*

- **Asaph** (a Jewish name) was keeper of the king's *pardes* (a Persian word meaning a planted park or pleasure ground, whence our English "paradise"). This was a royal forest or park near Jerusalem, not the distant Lebanon forest. (Ellicott, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/2.htm; Pulpit Commentary, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/nehemiah-2.html)

- The timber was for three purposes: (1) the **gates of the citadel** (*birah*) — the fortress at the northwest angle of the temple area that protected the temple (later known in Roman times as the Antonia Fortress); (2) the **city wall**; and (3) **Nehemiah's own residence** as governor. (Ellicott; Constable, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/nehemiah-2.html)

- Constable notes there were also **good political reasons** for Artaxerxes to grant the request: revolts in Egypt and Syria had been recently put down, and a strengthened, loyal Judah would help stabilize the region and provide a bulwark on the Egyptian border. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/nehemiah-2.html)

- **"The gracious hand of my God was upon me"** — this is Nehemiah's theological interpretation of events. He attributes the king's favorable response not to luck, politics, or his own skill, but to God's sovereign goodness. As Proverbs 21:1 states, "The king's heart is like channels of water in the hand of the LORD." (Guzik, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-2/; PreceptAustin excerpt via search)

- The Pulpit Commentary Homiletics section notes: "Many fail in this. Even those who have prayed for what they have received do not always make due acknowledgment. Thanksgivings are not so plentiful as prayers." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/nehemiah-2.html)

---

## v. 9 — Journey with Military Escort

*Then I went to the governors west of the Euphrates and gave them the king's letters. The king had also sent army officers and cavalry with me.*

- Nehemiah **actually went**. Guzik stresses: "Many people have a heart touched like Nehemiah's…but they stop short of actually going out and doing." The 800-mile (1,300 km) journey required real commitment. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-2/)

- The **military escort** (army officers and cavalry) was provided by the king. The Bridgeway Commentary contrasts this with Ezra, who had refused a military escort (Ezra 8:21–23), but notes that circumstances were different and Nehemiah felt it wise to accept the offer. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/nehemiah-2.html)

- The journey, which would have taken about three months, is passed over in silence in the narrative, as Ezra's had been. (Ellicott, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/2.htm)

- The Pulpit Commentary speculates that one of these governors was **Adieus**, satrap of Syria, named by Josephus. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/nehemiah-2.html)

---

## v. 10 — First Opposition: Sanballat and Tobiah

*But when Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the Ammonite official heard about this, they were deeply disturbed that someone had come to seek the well-being of the Israelites.*

- **Sanballat the Horonite** — likely from one of the Beth-horons (Upper or Lower), in the region of Samaria. The Elephantine papyri name him as governor of Samaria. His name is Babylonian in origin. (Ellicott; Constable, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/nehemiah-2.html; Pulpit Commentary, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/nehemiah-2.html)

- **Tobiah the Ammonite official** — the Hebrew name means "Yahweh is good," suggesting Jewish ancestry. He was either a native Ammonite chief who had been a servant at the Persian court, or (more likely per Ellicott) a servant and counsellor of Sanballat. (Ellicott; Constable; Pulpit Commentary)

- The phrase **"deeply disturbed"** (literally "it grieved them exceedingly") reflects that the revival of Jerusalem threatened Samaria's regional ascendency. Since Zerubbabel had rejected Samaritan cooperation (Ezra 4:3), enmity between the two peoples had been ongoing. (Pulpit Commentary; Ellicott)

- Guzik notes an important principle: **opposition did not arise** during the heart-stage, vision-stage, prayer-stage, or planning-stage — but only when Nehemiah actually began *doing* something. "Our spiritual enemies don't mind as long as all we do is plan and pray and talk; but when God's people start doing something, they take notice." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-2/)

- The Bridgeway Commentary adds that officials who previously controlled the Jerusalem district were hostile because Nehemiah, besides being Jewish, had authority from the Persian king that made him independent of them. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/nehemiah-2.html)

---

## v. 11 — Three Days of Waiting in Jerusalem

*After I had arrived in Jerusalem and had been there three days…*

- Following the example of Ezra (Ezra 8:32), Nehemiah rested **three days** after the long journey before taking any action. Ellicott says this was "for rest and devotion…to review the past and prepare for the future." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/2.htm)

- Guzik draws a leadership lesson: "Nehemiah traveled to Jerusalem, full of heart, full of prayer, full of faith, full of wisdom, full of a big vision, full of support from the king. When he finally got to his destination, **he did nothing for three days**." Good leaders learn God's timing. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-2/)

- Constable includes this as one of Donald Campbell's "21 principles of effective leadership": Nehemiah "took time (three days) to rest, pray, and plan." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/nehemiah-2.html)

---

## v. 12 — The Secret Nighttime Inspection Begins

*I set out at night with a few men. I did not tell anyone what my God had laid on my heart to do for Jerusalem. The only animal with me was the one on which I was riding.*

- Nehemiah chose **secrecy** for two reasons: (1) he wanted to avoid alerting enemies before his plans were ready, and (2) he wanted to formulate a plan before the Jews could marshal arguments against rebuilding. (Constable, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/nehemiah-2.html)

- The phrase **"what my God had laid on my heart"** is significant. Nehemiah understood his burden as divinely placed — not mere human ambition. (Guzik, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-2/)

- Guzik quotes Spurgeon: "You will often find it best not to commit your plans to others. If you want to serve God, go and do it, and then let other people find it out afterwards." He also quotes Redpath: "It is good to have Christian friends, but it is dangerous to wear your heart on your sleeve." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-2/)

- The Pulpit Commentary notes that all arrangements were made to **avoid notice**: Nehemiah went out by night, with few attendants, and only one beast. He wished to see the extent of the repairs needed with his own eyes but wanted as few as possible to know. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/nehemiah-2.html)

---

## v. 13 — The Route: Valley Gate, Serpent Well, Dung Gate

*So I went out at night through the Valley Gate toward the Well of the Serpent and the Dung Gate, and I inspected the walls of Jerusalem that had been broken down and the gates that had been destroyed by fire.*

- **The Valley Gate** opened on the Valley of Hinnom, to the south or southwest of the city. It was one of the gates Uzziah had fortified (2 Chronicles 26:9). (Ellicott, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/2.htm; Pulpit Commentary)

- **The Dragon Well** (or Serpent Well) is "nowhere else mentioned, and not now to be traced." Dean Stanley suggested it may be the pool of Siloam, with a legend about a dragon's mouth controlling the intermittent flow, but this is uncertain. (Ellicott; Pulpit Commentary, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/nehemiah-2.html)

- **The Dung Gate** (or Refuse Gate) was situated toward the middle of the southern wall, outside of which lay the sweepings and offscourings of the streets. (Pulpit Commentary)

- The word translated **"inspected"** or "viewed" is a medical term — it was used for **probing a wound** to see the extent of its damage. Nehemiah was not sightseeing; he was making a careful diagnosis. (Guzik, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-2/)

- Guzik suggests Nehemiah set out from the **west side** of the city, then turned south, continuing counterclockwise around the rubble. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-2/)

---

## v. 14 — Fountain Gate and King's Pool; Impassable Rubble

*Then I went on to the Fountain Gate and the King's Pool, but there was no room for the animal under me to get through…*

- **The Fountain Gate** is near the pool of Siloam (called "the king's pool" here), probably the "gate between two walls" of 2 Kings 25:4. (Ellicott, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/2.htm; Pulpit Commentary, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/nehemiah-2.html)

- **"There was no room for the animal under me to pass"** — the accumulated rubble was so great that Nehemiah had to dismount and proceed on foot, even in the darkness. (Pulpit Commentary)

- Constable suggests that Nehemiah may have only surveyed the **southern parts** of Jerusalem's wall because those were the only sections still standing. Jerusalem was always attacked from the north, so little was preserved in that direction. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/nehemiah-2.html)

---

## v. 15 — Up the Valley, Completing the Circuit

*…so I went up the valley by night and inspected the wall. Then I headed back and reentered through the Valley Gate.*

- **"The valley"** or "brook" is the Kidron Valley, which skirted the city on the east. From there Nehemiah could look up at the eastern wall along its whole length and see its condition. (Pulpit Commentary, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/nehemiah-2.html)

- Following the brook, Nehemiah reached the northeastern angle of the city, then turned back, skirting the northern wall, and reentered by the Valley Gate — thus **completing the circuit** of the walls. (Pulpit Commentary; Ellicott, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/2.htm)

- Again the word **"inspected"** is the medical term for probing a wound. Nehemiah was counting the cost. Guzik: "He has a heart, he has faith, he has a vision – but before that vision can become a reality, he must see exactly what has to be done, and what it will cost – in terms of time, effort, money, and leadership." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-2/)

---

## v. 16 — Complete Secrecy Maintained

*The officials did not know where I had gone or what I was doing, for I had not yet told the Jews or priests or nobles or officials or any other workers.*

- Nehemiah kept his mission secret from **everyone** — Jews, priests, nobles, officials, and "the rest that did the work" (meaning those who would later become the builders). (Ellicott)

- The Pulpit Commentary notes that the city "teemed with elements of danger" and the nobles and rulers possessed "no substantial repressive authority." Secrecy was justified by later events. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/nehemiah-2.html)

- Constable observes that this secrecy allowed Nehemiah to formulate his plan before the Jews could marshal arguments against it. When he did present his ideas (vv. 17–18), the people responded positively — evidence of his wisdom as a leader. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/nehemiah-2.html)

---

## v. 17 — Nehemiah's Rallying Speech

*Then I said to them, “You see the trouble we are in. Jerusalem lies in ruins, and its gates have been burned down. Come, let us rebuild the wall of Jerusalem, so that we will no longer be a disgrace.”*

- The original contains **no note of time** — not even the word "then." Nehemiah simply says, "And I said to them." When his plans were matured, he made an earnest appeal. (Ellicott, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/2.htm; Pulpit Commentary)

- Nehemiah began by identifying himself **with** the people: "**we** are in…trouble…**we** will no longer be a disgrace." He didn't blame them for the 100-year-old problem. Guzik: "He described the problem without blaming anyone else. When we fail to do this, there's a word for it: gossip." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-2/)

- The phrase **"that we may no longer be a reproach"** appealed to a need they all felt: a defenseless Jerusalem was a joke to the surrounding neighbors. (PreceptAustin excerpt via search)

- Guzik notes: "The citizens and leaders of Jerusalem were not sitting around waiting for a hero to rebuild their walls. Probably, they had come to accept that it was an impossible job." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-2/)

---

## v. 18 — The People's Enthusiastic Response

*I also told them about the gracious hand of my God upon me, and what the king had said to me. “Let us start rebuilding,” they replied, and they set their hands to this good work.*

- Nehemiah did not rely on his own eloquence alone. He **told them two things**: (1) how God's providence had guided him, and (2) the king's actual words of permission. The king's commission removed the danger of being accused of rebellion. (Pulpit Commentary, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/nehemiah-2.html; Ellicott)

- The people's response was immediate and unified: **"Let us rise up and build."** The Hebrew of "they strengthened their hands for this good work" is briefer and more emphatic — literally, "they strengthened their hands for good." They embraced the good cause heartily. (Pulpit Commentary)

- The Bridgeway Commentary notes: "This first-hand knowledge, together with his account of how God had guided all the events leading up to his return, convinced the people that they should start rebuilding the walls." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/nehemiah-2.html)

- Guzik emphasizes that Nehemiah succeeded because he **didn't just pray, plan, and talk; he actually went and did the work.** "It is one thing to stand around with other believers and talk about doing some evangelism…it is another thing to actually go out and do it." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-2/)

---

## v. 19 — The Opposition Escalates: Mockery and Accusation

*But when Sanballat the Horonite, Tobiah the Ammonite official, and Geshem the Arab heard about this, they mocked us and ridiculed us, saying, “What is this you are doing? Are you rebelling against the king?”*

- **Geshem the Arab** now appears, completing the triumvirate of opposition leaders. Ellicott describes him as "probably the leader of an Arabian company," while Constable notes that far from being negligible, he was an even more powerful figure than his companions — he and his son ruled a league of Arabian tribes controlling Moab, Edom, parts of Arabia, and the approaches to Egypt. (Ellicott, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/2.htm; Constable, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/nehemiah-2.html)

- The opposition **escalated** from being "deeply disturbed" (v. 10) to open mockery and a charge of treason. Their question — **"Are you rebelling against the king?"** — was a cunning political attack, since Artaxerxes himself had previously ordered the work stopped (Ezra 4:21). The same accusation would reappear in Nehemiah 6:6. (Ellicott; Pulpit Commentary, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/nehemiah-2.html)

- The Pulpit Commentary suggests these three may not have been independent chieftains residing on three sides of Judah, but rather Sanballat was the satrap and both Tobiah and Geshem were in his service — Tobiah as counsellor, Geshem as leader of Arab troops maintained at Samaria. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/nehemiah-2.html)

---

## v. 20 — Nehemiah's Bold Answer: God Will Prosper Us

*So I answered them and said, “The God of heaven is the One who will grant us success. We, His servants, will start rebuilding, but you have no portion, right, or claim in Jerusalem.”*

- Nehemiah's response is remarkable for what it **does not** include: he does not mention the king's permission, does not produce the royal letters, and does not defend himself point-by-point against the charge of rebellion. The Pulpit Commentary wonders whether he thought revealing the truth would drive them to some desperate attempt. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/nehemiah-2.html)

- Instead, Nehemiah claims **divine sanction**: "The God of heaven, He will prosper us." This echoes Zerubbabel's earlier answer to Tattenai: "We are the servants of the God of heaven and earth" (Ezra 5:11). (Pulpit Commentary; Ellicott, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/2.htm)

- The closing words — **"you have no portion, nor right, nor memorial in Jerusalem"** — imply that the Samaritan enemies, as in Zerubbabel's day, desired to have a share in the undertaking. Nehemiah strengthens Zerubbabel's earlier refusal: they have nothing in common with Jerusalem, not even a place in its memorials, save one of shame. (Ellicott)

- Constable notes that Nehemiah thus continued the policy begun by Zerubbabel of **not allowing the people of the land to help rebuild** (Ezra 4:3), and he trusted in God's enabling power rather than his own ability. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/nehemiah-2.html)

- Guzik observes: "Nehemiah ignored their scorn. His bold, straightforward words showed he had not been put on the defensive by their mocking, scornful attack." He simply proclaimed confidence in God and refused to let enemies distract him from the work. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-2/)

- The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary adds: "Nehemiah's answer was based on confident faith in God…Because they trusted Him they would build the wall without fail. The three detractors had nothing in Jerusalem; no part, no right, no memorial." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/nehemiah-2.html)

## Summary of Key Themes Across Traditions

1. **Prayer and Planning belong together** — all traditions agree. The four months of prayer (1:1 → 2:1) combined with careful, detailed planning is a model of godly leadership.

2. **The "arrow prayer" of v. 4** is universally noted as a beautiful example of continual communion with God, resting on a foundation of extended prior prayer.

3. **Opposition as confirmation** — Guzik and Bloom both stress that opposition arose only when action began, and that opposition is not a sign of being out of God's will.

4. **Nehemiah's wisdom and tact** — all commentators highlight his careful speech (avoiding "Jerusalem" at first), his secrecy, his identification with the people, and his boldness in asking for resources.

5. **The theological center** is v. 8b and v. 20: "the good hand of my God" and "the God of heaven…will prosper us." Nehemiah attributes everything to God's sovereign grace, not human skill or political maneuvering.
